1.	No person sent from England to Canada for internment came to Canada under the classification of "anti-Fascist'' or "anti-Nazi". All civilians sent from England to Canada for internment were described as "civilian internees". Subsequent to the internment of the persons so sent, an official of the home office came to Canada and brought with him dossiers relating to individual cases. This official between November, 1940 and June 1941 investigated the cases of civilian internees and arranged for the return of some 700 of them to England. speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRISONERS OF WAR
speechtext:
1. The protecting power for Canadian interests in Germany and Italy is Switzerland. The
responsibility of the Swiss authorities for the protection of Canadian interests in these countries includes the protection of all members of the Canadian forces taken prisoner by Germany and Italy.
2.	The Canadian minister at Washington has expressed to the department of state the gratitude of the Canadian government for services rendered by the United States as the protecting power for Canadian interests in Germany and Italy and in territories occupied by Germany and Italy.
3.	It is not possible to say what neutral countries might be available to serve as protecting powers for Canadian interests should further occasion arise. The Canadian government is and has been taking parallel action with the governments of the United Kingdom and of the other dominions for the protection of members of the Canadian forces taken prisoner by the enemy through the protecting powers for Canadian interests and through the International Red Cross Committee at Geneva. The specific arrangements made are those provided for by the International Prisoner of War Convention of 1929.
4.	As stated in reply to question 1 Switzerland has assumed the protection of Canadian interests in Germany and Italy and German and Italian occupied territories. This responsibility includes the inspection of prisoner of war camps where Canadians are held and making arrangements for the exchange of sick and wounded prisoners of war. Argentina as the protecting power for Canadian interests in Japan and Manchuria exercises a similar responsibility there.
5.	Argentina is the protecting power for Canadian interests in Japan and Manchuria. Switzerland is the protecting power for Canadian interests in occupied China. subtopic: TRANSFERS FROM ARMY TO AIR FORCE
speechtext:

On transfer from army to air force a man must be medically examined, his army pay adjusted, uniform and equipment turned in and deficiencies accounted for by the soldier, and formalities of discharge from the army, including discharge certificate, completed. There must be liaison between the commanding officer of the soldier's unit and the air force recruiting officer. While at the advanced training centre, or on home defence service, the man cannot enlist in the air force unless he has made application therefor before commencing basic training, and the district officer commanding consents. After the man is made into a trained soldier and has become an integral part of an army he would not be allowed to transfer to the air force unless there were special reasons why it should be done.

subtopic: CANADIAN FLAG
speechtext:
1.	It is substantially correct to say that Canada declared war with other countries in 1939, 1940 and 1941 as an autonomous country and independently of the United' Kingdom. It would, perhaps, <oe more correct to say that, following upon the decision of the parliament of Canada, advice was tendered to His Majesty the King by the Prime Minister of Canada. Pursuant to this advice, His Majesty approved the issuing of proclamations in Canada in his name declaring the existence of a state of war with Canada in the following cases: (a) Germany, September 10, 1939; (b) Italy, June 10, 1940; (c) Hungary, Roumania and Finland, December 7, 1941; (d) Japan, December 7, 1941.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: KIRKLAND LAKE MINERS-QUESTION OF DISCRIMINATION AND PRESERVATION OF SENIORITY RIGHTS
speechtext:
I wish to ask a question of the Minister of Labour. I sent a copy of it to the Secretary of State, not knowing that the Minister of Labour would be in his seat to-day. It arises out of a telegram received this morning from one of the officials of the Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers' union of Kirkland Lake, a copy of which I understand is in the hands of the Minister of Labour.
My information is that a formula was worked out between the Department of Labour, the union and the operators, to the effect that on termination of the strike the men were to return to work without discrimination, and that the rule of seniority would be observed as far as possible. This understanding is not being lived up to by the operators. Rank discrimination is being practised, and an intolerable situation is developing. In view of the fact that the Department of Labour negotiated the return to work and is a party to that agreement, what is the Department of Labour doing to see that the terms of the agreement are being enforced?

subtopic: KIRKLAND LAKE MINERS-QUESTION OF DISCRIMINATION AND PRESERVATION OF SENIORITY RIGHTS
speechtext:
The fact is that the strikers returned to work in greater numbers than could be absorbed by the mines. In view of the departure of several hundred miners from the area during the strike, and the consequent reduction in employment available for surface workers, the men returned unconditionally without intervention by the Department of Labour. A delegation of miners did wait on the Acting Minister of Labour (Mr, McLarty) and asked that the department should seek to have the men reemployed without discrimination. On February 14 the department sent the following telegram to Mr. Robert Bryce, president of Macassa Mines and chairman of the operators' committee:
Minister of Labour has been asked to request the Kirkland Lake mining companies that as men return to work they be reemployed without discrimination and that seniority rights be respected. Minister would appreciate a statement in reply.
On February 16 Mr. Bryce sent the following telegram in reply:
As the reopening of various sections of the mines permits the procedure outlined in your telegram to me being followed as closely as possible having due and proper regard for the efficiency and safety of the operations.
Representations contained in the telegram from Mr. James Rankin, vice-president of the Kirkland Lake local, have been referred by the departmental officials to the mining authorities, and when further information is available I shall be glad to give it to my hon. friend.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Well, I cannot face all parts of the house. I have only one face, and I believe I should speak to the Chair. However I shall do the best I can to have hon. members hear me.
I first ask the government to give the house and country a straightforward pronouncement indicating what action they will take if the plebiscite is decided in the affirmative. I think we have the right to know that, and I say the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) owes it to the country to tell it that much. Up to date he has studiously avoided giving any indication of the government's proposals. I tell him now, as I told him before, that that is not good enough, and that the people of Canada expect something more.
The Prime Minister has at his disposal all the facts of the situation. He is in a position to forecast the future requirements of our forces, and the means by which it will be necessary to raise them. We have not that information. We are entitled to those facts, and to a government pronouncement concerning them.
I therefore put this direct question to the Prime Minister: If and when he is released from his past commitments, what action has he in view? I request an answer to that
/84	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
question. Surely he must be in a position to tell that to the house and country. Does he not think the people of Canada are entitled to know what his intentions are, before they vote on the plebiscite? Unless the people know his intentions they will be voting blindly, voting to give him a -blank cheque. What'direction or leadership is there in that procedure? What enlightenment have the people of Canada received from the Prime Minister as to why they should vote yea or nay?
Further, I believe the Prime Minister should tell the house and country what he will do if the result of the plebiscite is indecisive- that is, if there should be a very small majority in favour of releasing him from his commitments, or a small majority the other way. Will he take the attitude of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, at the time of the temperance plebiscite, and say that a small majority does not give him a mandate to proceed with his proposals, notwithstanding the fact that the enemy may be knocking at our doors?
Last night I listened to a radio broadcast. With some of it I agreed, and with some I did not agree. It was an address by Professor Thompson of Manitoba university. Among other things he said that the week Singapore fell was the blackest week in a whole century. I agreed with that. Yet here we are, twiddling about a plebiscite to release the Prime Minister.
I place this question before him: Suppose that only fifty per cent of the qualified electors cast a ballot on this plebiscite, and as a result only twenty-seven per cent or thirty per cent of the total electorate favour the release of the government from its past commitments-and that may well happen-what will the Prime Minister do? I have known of general elections in my own constituency where not more than sixty per cent of the people voted, and I fear that is what will happen in the present instance. How will the government interpret a vote of, we will say, twenty-seven per cent of the total electorate?
These are questions which naturally arise in the minds of all of us. Here is another situation which I can visualize, and which may very well happen-and I wonder if the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) would be good enough to lower his voice. If he is going to talk in this chamber while an hon. member is on his feet, then I suggest he should lower his voice, or leave the chamber. I cannot continue if the minister continues his talking too. Only one of us can talk at a time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I am talking to one of your
supporters.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
My supporter is a very reasonable man, and usually the minister is too. But it is very disquieting to have to hear the minister, even if he is talking to a gentleman as high placed in my affections as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), when I am trying to make a reasoned argument.
Here is another question I put to the Prime Minister: What will happen if the plebiscite carries by a large majority in seven or eight provinces, and is defeated in one or two? How will the Prime Minister interpret that result? Will he feel at liberty to proceed with his proposals-if he has any to make- or will those proposals be abandoned? That is something about which we should be informed. The house and country are entitled to know the answers to these questions.
Then, I put this further question to the Prime Minister: If there is a large majority, a substantial majority or, indeed, any majority, against the release of the Prime Minister from his commitments, what will he do then? Will he interpret this result to mean that his government has no mandate to defend Canada, the empire and the whole family of allied nations, to the last man and the last dollar?-and it may well come to that. Or will he interpret it to mean that his government has lost the confidence of the people? What will he do in these circumstances?
These are questions which are bothering the Canadian people and, I am sure, bothering hon. members in the house, even those who blindly follow the administration.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: No.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Yes, some of them blindly follow the administration; and wrhen I say that I do not believe I am putting the case too strongly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: They never had their eyes opened.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
If one were to recall the adulation heaped upon the Prime Minister by some of his followers in the country, one would think that he was omnipotent. I should think that the Prime Minister if he had any-I shall not use the word I might use-I should think he would be revolted by such adulation as I have heard coming from hon. members opposite. To me it would be most embarrassing. The Prime Minister would be the first man to admit that he is only human, and that he has as many-

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
imperfections as most of us. I say that hon. members opposite blindly follow their leader, without any why or wherefore.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: So do the people.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: So much the worse for the people, then.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: You have not talked to them all yet.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: A reasoned and informed public opinion in Canada is something that we want. I am afraid throughout the country there is too much blind complacency-the blind following the blind. There is a lot of it. Public opinion in Canada needs an awakening to the true position of affairs. They are beginning to awaken on the east coast. Where are the two members for Halifax? Where are they to-day? We may hear from them to-morrow. They have been called down by their constituents, and the question of the defence of the east coast is being put up to these two hon. gentlemen, not by any partisan committee, but by the people of Halifax, who know that it is not possible to guarantee the defence of their fair city. They are alarmed about it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: They are better off than in other parts of the province.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: I daresay they are, but that does not mean much. I do not mean to be an alarmist. I do not believe the people of Halifax are in immediate danger of invasion. I should think that invasion of the east coast of Canada is one of the most remote possibilities, although the escape of the German battleships from Brest is a menace to the Atlantic coast. There is a certain amount of danger of a sporadic attack on the city of Halifax, as there is on the city of Vancouver.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: And on Port Darwin.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Port Darwin is nearer to the Japanese forces. But a sporadic attack on our coasts is a possibility. Therefore I think the people of this country have a right to know what are the government's proposals in a given case. I have instanced three or four of them, and I ask the Prime Minister to tell, when he comes to speak on this resolution, if he does, what the government are going to do about these things. Will he tell the people what will be done in certain eventualities? Or are the people to be content to follow blindly, trusting in the Prime Minister-trusting in the Prime Minister whose aim, as long as I can remember, has been to assume and continue to hold political power. That has been the
chief ambition of my right hon. friend all through his lifetime. If you do not believe me, I call to your attention a book which has recently appeared in this country, written by Mr. Bruce Hutchison. Read what he says- and he is not an unfriendly critic of the Prime Minister.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: He is no authority.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I do not even know the gentleman except to see him, but I would think he is a student of public affairs and of Canadian political history. I commend to hon. gentlemen the reading of that book, and if I can help sell a few copies for him, so much the better.
There is another question I want to ask the government. What will be the attitude of the Prime Minister and of his cabinet colleagues while the plebiscite campaign is proceeding? Will they campaign for a favourable vote, or will they campaign against releasing the government from its obligations? Both questions are pertinent having regard to what must be the division in public opinion in certain quarters in this country.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: What will the leader of the opposition do?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
I am going to tell you before I am through. I am not entitled to be put on the spot at this moment, but I am going to be frank. I am going to tell the people of this country and the Conservative party that they should vote yes, without any question. Then, if the Prime Minister and the government do not proceed, we will turn on the heat just as strong as we can, so that this country shall have an all-out war effort.
What will the government do while the plebiscite campaign is proceeding? I ask again these two questions: Will they campaign to release the government? Will they campaign to defeat the object of the plebiscite? What will the Minister of Transport (Mr. Cardin) do? I ask him now, where is he going to be on this plebiscite?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: I have no hesitation in answering my hon. friend. I find it extraordinary that he should ask such a question of me. I am a member of the government and I stand with the government. If I were not taking that attitude I would not be entitled to the position I hold in the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: I have not understood yet what the minister's attitude is.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
It is very clear.
786	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: If I interpret the minister correctly, he is going out to campaign to release the government from its pledge?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Certainly.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: And then what will he do, if the government is released?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: As much as my hon. friend will do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
As much as I will do? The minister knows exactly where I stand in regard to releasing the government. I have stated my position. But if the government are released, then what? Where will the Minister of Transport be then?
Will the Prime Minister and his colleagues address meetings and give radio broadcasts during the campaign? What opportunity will be provided for leaders and representatives of other parties in this house, and other bodies of public opinion in this country, to express their views over the national radio network?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Is the hon. member going to oppose it?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
The minister evidently was not listening. He is not informed; he is not up to date. What opportunity, I ask, will be provided for the leaders of other parties in this country and other bodies of public opinion to express their views over the radio, free of charge, just as the government does? That is a pertinent question, and I desire to press it. What facilities will be afforded to me to tell the people of Canada over the radio, when the time arrives, what I think they ought to do? This is a question which I think should be answered while the resolution is still under discussion and before the bill is introduced. That is all I have to ask the Prime Minister at the moment, but some other questions may occur to me as I go along.
The Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) estimated that the cost of the plebiscite would be one and a half million dollars. I am going to ask him to give us a break-down of that amount when we get into committee, and I give him notice now. I fear it will be very much more than a million and a half dollars-and it will be a million and a half dollars of the taxpayers' money which will be absolutely wasted unless we have some assurance that the government will act on the plebiscite vote.
When will the plebiscite be held? I think we ought to have more specific information on that point. Time, I suggest, is an allimportant factor, and under conditions as

they exist to-day, if the plebiscite must be taken, I urge that it be taken at the earliest possible day.
I welcome the announcement that all soldiers, including those who are under twenty-one years of age, will be allowed to vote. I ask the Secretary of State this question: I assume that the vote will be taken under the jurisdiction of his department?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Under the chief electoral officer.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: To whom does he report?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: The Secretary of State is only a contact point between him and the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
He is the man to direct the vote. There must be somebody here as spokesman of the chief electoral officer, and I am taking it for granted that the Secretary of State is that spokesman; therefore I am asking him to give us some information as to how the vote will be taken in England. What arrangements will be made to take the votes of airmen and others who are in far distant theatres of war such as Libya and Burma? They are entitled to vote, just as much as a soldier in Newfoundland.
I come to another important proposition. If the plebiscite is carried in the affirmative, will the Prime Minister bring his detailed proposals, if any, for increased effort as regards the mobilization of man-power-I am for the moment limiting it to that, but it need not necessarily be so limited, it should probably cover the whole gamut of mobilization, not only of man-power but of wealth and material resources-to the House of Commons, where chey may be passed upon, and where they ought to be passed upon? Or will he merely seek the repeal of section 3, the limiting clause of the mobilization act, and then institute his policies by order in council? If this is to be done by order in council, I object. Whatever may have been said of the Military Service Act of 1917, the proposals were brought down to parliament and they were debated here and they were improved here. That is the only democratic way of doing it. In other words, will the Prime Minister interpret an affirmative result as giving the government a free hand, or merely as giving parliament a free hand? There is a distinction between the two. In my view any proposals which may follow the plebiscite should be brought down to this house and passed in the form of legislation. so that the people's representatives may have something to say about them.

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hanson (York-Sunbury)
I believe there is a terrible sense of frustration on the part of private members of this house. They have not a word to say about this question of mobilizing man-power, wealth or material resources. Why, they are not even rubber stamps, because all these things are done by order in council, and they never know a word about anything-good, bad, or indifferent-until it is all over.
Mr. McDONALD (Pontiacl: What a herol

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Well, if the hon. member has courage enough to stand up and make his interjection, let him make it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Quite a hero!

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Well, I never posed as a hero, but I have never been a rubber stamp, and I never will be.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that to institute by order in council any elaborate scheme of compulsory service of man-power or of mobilization of resources and wealth would be quite improper, no matter how extensive may be the powers of the governor in council in that respect.
I now desire to make a few brief observations on the concrete proposals as indicated by the Secretary of State.
The modus operandi is to be governed not so much by legislation as by the regulations authorized by the legislation. I believe that is a correct interpretation of what he had to say. Now our ordinary election law is fully covered by the Dominion Elections Act, and I want to point out to the minister and to hon. members that the regulations passed under that act, speaking generally, are interpretative, not legislative. Under this proposed act the regulations will not be interpretative; they will be legislative. Is that not a correct statement, and does it not accurately interpret the minister's position? If that be true, I think, it is wrong in principle and it is derogating from the powers of this parliament that we should delegate by this bill of ten sections power to legislate by order in council. God knows we have had enough of that in this country. This is not a war matter. It is not something which is being dealt with under the War Measures Act. It is being dealt with by parliament up to a limited point. Why should any legislative functions be left to the governor in council to be passed under regulation? I put that question to hon. gentlemen, and to the minister. Is it too much to ask that the policy of the law be changed to conform to that of the Dominion Elections Act? That is all I am asking for. It is a matter of principle. I ask the minister to take that into consideration. If, however, the government is to go on and legislate by regulation, then I do suggest to
the members of this committee which is to be, that they will have to exercise the greatest possible care in framing the regulations, and I express the hope that the committee will examine them very carefully.
I was glad to learn-I think I am correct in this assumption-that the regulations as drafted to date are not immutable. I believe the minister used that very word. Otherwise there could not be any point in referring them to a committee. We have that assurance, that they are subject to review, and I hope that review will be given to them by this committee. But let not the Secretary of State lose sight for one moment of the point I have just raised, that under the elections act the regulations are interpretative, not legislative; under the proposed act they are legislative and not specially interpretative-and that, I think, is wrong. To my mind it is a defect in the bill.
Until we have the detailed provisions of the bill I do not wish to comment on the question of qualification and disqualification of voters. That is a matter which has often been the subject of debate in this house. There are particular situations which will have to be dealt with with great care; there are certain people who ought to vote, and certain people who ought not to vote. At this moment I am going to make just one suggestion to the minister in the utmost good faith, and based, I think, on principle. In August, 1940, we had a national registration, when our population, male and female, above the age of sixteen years were all required to register. By the way, that registration cost something like $900,000- quite a substantial sum. I wonder if we have had value received for it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
The work was mostly
voluntary.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
And, a
good deal of the work was done voluntarily, as I am reminded and as I happen to know from personal observation. However, I have often had doubt whether that registration was one hundred per cent complete. I do not know. Some estimate, I suppose, might be formed by the bureau of statistics, the people who had charge of the census and so on. But I would urge upon the government that it be a condition precedent, so far as the civilian vote in Canada is concerned, that every voter who presents himself for the ballot produce his registration certificate, and that unless he or she does so he or she shall not vote. I urge the government to adopt this suggestion. The reason is obvious. Anyone who has not registered and complied with the law may properly be classed as a shirker, and no shirker should be allowed to vote on this plebiscite.
788	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Hanson ( York-Sanbury)
In respect of the other aspects of disqualification I shall reserve further comment.
From the minister's statement, I observe that a new electoral list is to be compiled. From something I saw in the newspapers a while back I was very fearful that the government were contemplating using the lists of the 1940 elections, and I called attention to it at that time. I was told that the matter had not been considered, or something to that effect. These lists of course are two years old and they would be most unsuitable, and for the reason that the minister gave. I desire to correct myself on the question of statistics. I had in mind just the males coming of age. I find that in the year 1941 approximately 107,000 males attained the age of 21, and 106,000 females, making a total of 213,000, or in two years 426,000. The ten year average it stated to be 204,000 per annum, so that since the 1940 lists were made up nearly half a million voters have come of age. That is a large number and they are undoubtedly entitled to vote.
Then there is the question of change in the location of population, to which the Secretary of State made reference. All these considerations make it imperative that a new list should be compiled, and I commend the government for that decision.
On the question of open or closed lists, there are two views. I have always favoured open lists for rural areas, where everyone knows everybody else and where there is not a chance, not one in a thousand, of any electoral fraud. But with respect to urban areas, I am of a contrary opinion. I think there ought to be closed lists there, even if there is to be a revision. There is no danger in the rural areas, but there is a very grave danger in certain urban localities. One has but to follow the history of elections in one of the great cities of this country to visualize what will happen if the principle of open lists is to be followed in all the large urban areas, and I do beg the government to reconsider this aspect even if it should involve the cost of revision in urban areas and some little delay and expense.
There are one or two other things that have bothered me about the plebiscite. Who is to man the polls and see that the law is complied with, and that people do not vote who are not entitled to vote? I do not know whether consideration has been given to this question. Then there is another question. How in winter or in early spring are the voters to be drawn to the polls? I know the answer will be that there is no provision in the law now, and I do not suggest that there should be. But let us not delude ourselves.
I have run seven or eight elections myself.

Hon. gentlemen opposite and around me have all run elections, and they know that the biggest problem is getting the people to the polls.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Most of them will be walking at that time.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
They will not walk; that is just the point. I remember sending a horse and buggy once for a woman to come to the poll and she absolutely refused to come unless she could be brought in a fine motor car. That is the attitude of people. They do not want to come and vote. Who is to get them out? I do not suggest that the government should arrange to have them driven to the polls. It is against the law now, I believe. But that is a provision of the law that is more honoured in the breach than the observance, and we all know it in our hearts. Why continue it in the statute? I suggest,, however, that some provision should be made with regard to scrutineers. That would not cost a great deal. I have nothing further to offer on that line at the moment, but I do know that it is important.
My learned and hon. friend the member for Regina city (Mr. McNiven) rather anticipated in his question what I am about to say now. Since this whole proposal was mooted I have given serious and rather continuous thought to the attitude that I should take with regard to the matter. One's first reaction is to say, "to Hades with the thing," but that will not do. It is too serious. A responsibility rests upon me not only as a citizen of the country but as a member of this parliament occupying this position for the time being. I cannot ignore that responsibility. I just cannot do it. I have given consideration to what I should do. On Friday last the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysiborough (Mr. Kirk), who does not often take part in the debates in this house, suggested that I should go out and make the result decisive. Well, that is beyond my power, but I know what the hon. member meant, and he was well-intentioned. Then I asked him this question: Does the hon. member say that it is any responsibility of mine to go out and ask the people to vote for this plebiscite? I put it to him and he replied, I think, in the affirmative; and right off the bat, without stopping to consider and think as one ought to do, I said, "It is not my baby." Now, I do not wish anyone to infer that, because I am opposed to the holding of a plebiscite and do not wish to father it, I consider that to be the end of my responsibility. I do not.
Briefly, what is the position? The government is asking the people for a release from its pledge, given gratuitously and voluntarily,

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Noseworthy
and that it be allowed to take whatever course it desires. If the plebiscite is defeated the government will construe that position as indicating that it should not be released from its commitment-it may take that view. If the plebiscite carries we have no undertaking or guarantee that anything will be done. That appears to me to leave us all in an impossible position. I have a sense of frustration. The only person who wins anything in that is the Prime Minister. He is freed. Heads I win, tails you lose-or to put it in the reverse, heads he wins, tails I lose and the rest of us lose.
We ought not to be put in that position, but we are; and after the most mature reflection I cannot take the responsibility of advising anyone to vote no. because that would not only tie the hands of the government but would make it impossible for any further steps to be taken with regard to extending the man-power of the country for service beyond the territorial limitations of Canada. That I think is an impossible position for this country to occupy at this critical time. It should not be in that position.
On the other hand, if the vote carries we have absolutely no guarantee that anything will be done, and that brings to me a feeling of frustration. Neither of these positions is acceptable, but on the theory that if one has to make a decision and choose between the lesser of two evils, I am going to ask the people of the country to vote to release the government, and I now do so. I call upon the adherents of the Conservative party in Canada to go to the polls and vote yes on this plebiscite. That is the loyal and patriotic course. That is the course which may make possible the achievement of the objectives we have as a party.
As to what course I shall pursue to that end myself during the campaign on the plebiscite, I have not finally determined. I had thought of going to my own constituency, calling a public meeting, at my own expense, advertising it, asking the people to come, presenting to them the facts of the position as judicially as I could, and urging them to go to the polls and vote in the affirmative, in order that the government may be freed. If the government does not then act I notify them that the fight of the loyal people of this country' will just be beginning.
I do not propose to speak at any greater length at this time. In committee and during the various stages of the bill ample opportunity will be afforded for full discussion of the detailed proposals of the government. But I reiterate that I believe we should have at
this stage of the resolution a full statement from the Prime Minister in reply to the various questions I have asked.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
In these my first remarks in this house I want to thank all hon. members for the very warm welcome which was accorded me on the occasion of my introduction. I want also to thank the many members of parties other than my own for the assistance they have given me in the first few days of my presence here, assistance which helped to make my first days here much more pleasurable and less terrifying than they otherwise would have been.
I wish to make a few remarks on the resolution now before the house. I want to make these remarks now because, as hon. members know, I was absent, not being a member of the house, at the time the plebiscite was so fully discussed in connection with the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
During our recent campaign in York South the question of conscription of man-power for overseas service and of the plebiscite became a vital issue. My opponent in that campaign, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, went to bat first with a radio broadcast that concerned itself almost entirely with the question of conscription for overseas service. That was followed next day by the full-page advertisement of the total war committee. In that advertisement there were many definite references to conscription for overseas service, but in only one phrase in one line of that page was there anything definite about conscription of anything other than man-power. We, in our campaign, countered that move of our opponents by insisting that conscription of man-power for overseas service was only one phase, and not by any means the most important phase, of a total war effort. One issue that we kept before the electors coh-stantly was the need for the mobilization of everything necessary to win the war. From my experience in that campaign I am confident that the people of York South and-if they are representative, as I think they are, of the rest of Canada-the people of Canada will not by any means be satisfied with conscription of man-power only. Judging by letters which I have received both during my campaign and since the election from every province in Canada, from Liberals and Conservatives of long standing as well as from members of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, from office workers, professional men and women, labourers and farmers, labour organizations, and numerous other organizations, I am quite confident that this country is to-day ready for a much greater and much

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Noseworthy
more far-reaching war effort than anything that this government has undertaken or even envisioned.
During the latter weeks of our campaign I was constantly questioned regarding my stand on the plebiscite issue. My opponent chose, as the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) in this house has chosen, to oppose the taking of the plebiscite. At no time during the campaign did I take occasion to criticize the action of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his associates for the taking of that plebiscite. Nor did I find at anv time in that constituency, apart from the pro-conscriptionist press, any great indignation against the taking of the plebiscite. I found no such indignation expressed among the rank and file of the voters as I have heard expressed in this house by the leader of the official opposition. The people of York South-and I think they are representative of the people of Canada- are not nearly as much astounded at the phenomenon of the Prime Minister keeping his pledge to the electors as the opposition in this house appears to be.
What these people are really concerned about, and what they really want, is that all parties and all members of all parties should devote their combined intelligence and their combined energy to getting on with the business of winning the war. That is the business foremost in the minds of the people of the constituency from which I have just come.
I am personally convinced that the Prime Minister should be relieved of his electoral pledge. Furthermore, I am convinced that the only decent course he can follow is to appeal to the people of the country as he has chosen to do. As a matter of fact, the feeling of the people of York South on that point was so clear that my opponent was obliged to dissociate himself from his party or from the pledge that his party had given in .the 1940 election that there would be no conscription introduced if they were in power, that statement having been given during the election campaign. There was no criticism then. As a matter of fact, my opponent was challenged with the question, "Had not his party and its erstwhile leader of that period given the same pledge to the paople of Canada?"
I should like to see a great and overwhelming majority given to the government on the plebiscite. I feel confident that the government will receive that majority provided they are prepared to give to the people of this country, before the plebiscite is taken, a pledge in some form that they propose to

embark upon a genuine all-out war effort that will include a much greater mobilization of wealth than anything yet undertaken.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Why do hon. members on the government side not applaud that?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Such a pledge to gain the confidence and support of the Canadian people should, in my opinion, envision also a bold policy for the mobilization of industry.
The only fear as to the plebiscite that I ever heard expressed among the electors of my constituency was that a favourable vote would give the government the right to conscript man-power for farm, factory and the armed forces-and that power, I agree, they should possess in this crisis-but that it would leave the government free to carry on its present policy, which I term a policy of appeasement, with regard to wealth and industry.
I have read in the press that my opposition in the York South by-election are drawing some comfort from the myth that that election was directed by the government from Ottawa. I am amused by the fact that the official opposition place such confidence in the efficiency of that government direction. I am amused that they can accept that myth as an explanation of their loss of five thousand Conservative votes in the working class areas of that riding. The Prime Minister and his associates must, I am sure, feel quite elated over this compliment paid them by the official opposition.
Quite seriously, Mr. Speaker, that is not the answer to what happened in York South. The only intelligent answer is that the people of that constituency want an honest-to-goodness, all-out war effort. They are serious-minded people. They are deeply concerned, as all Canadians are concerned, about the winning of the war. They want more than a conscription bill which will enable the government to send men wherever they choose to send them. The working-class people of this country have already shown that they are ready to endure any sacrifice required of them in order to win this war; but they are sufficiently intelligent to know that something more is needed to win the war than the conscription of men for overseas service. I am fearful of the results of the plebiscite unless a pledge in some form can be given to indicate what other steps the government proposes to take in addition to the conscription of man-power. If the government wants the workers and farmers to give it a blank cheque-and I do not borrow that word from the leader of the opposition- that will enable it to use our man-power as

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Tucker
the government sees fit, then you must first create in the minds of the people a confidence that such power will never be used to exploit the working-class people of this country in the interests of any powerful group. You must convince the people that there is to be a much greater degree of equality of sacrifice than anything that has prevailed up to the present. You must also give the people the assurance that all industry is to be utilized for the war, regardless of the demand for private profit.
I should like to call attention for a moment, on this point, to a few statements reported in the Ottawa Morning Journal of to-day, from the recent radio broadcast by Sir Stafford Cripps. Speaking to the people who are unable to enlist for service, he is reported as having said:
. . . that those who "for age or other reasons" could not give their lives for their country "owe an obligation of service and devotion to the last ounce of our strength and the last dollar of our wealth."
Later, speaking of the situation in England, he said:
Personal interests are being allowed to obtrude themselves where the country's interest should be supreme, selfishness and the desire for petty profits sometimes taking the place of that all-embracing patriotism which leads our young men and women to give their lives for their country and its cause.
Then, speaking to Canadians, he asked this question:
But have you considered whether you in your country have yet realized how total must be the effort it required if the axis is to be conquered?	.
These words. I feel, express the wish and desire of the great majority of the Canadian people to-day. I can assure this house that across this country there is a seething dissatisfaction regarding our war effort. Not only have I met with it in my own riding; I have found it in hundreds of letters that I have received from every province since my election. That dissatisfaction does not rest on the failure of the government to secure enlistment for active service. Much of that sort of dissatisfaction I feel has been engendered in Canada by a pro-conscriptionist press.
The real dissatisfaction which exists in the minds of the people and which is wide-spread throughout this country, is the feeling that industry has not yet been geared to a maximum production for war purposes. I am told, for instance, that although we are in our third year of war we are not producing a single aeroplane engine for use in the planes that are to be used to defend our shores. That may or may not be correct. If it is correct, then I say it is a deplorable and regrettable
situation. There are to-day hundreds of industrial plants in and around Toronto alone which could and should be utilized for war production but which are still producing consumer goods for profit. I have received complaints from workers "by the dozen", if I may use a famous phrase, that they are obliged by force of circumstances to "rest on their oars" in- the matter of war production. I am told that the present cost-plus profit system that prevails in some of our war industries does not give opportunity to the workers to put forth their maximum effort. Men and foremen from munition and war industry plants around Toronto came to me in numbers during the election campaign, complaining that they were sick and tired of being forced to loaf on the job of war production in which they were engaged. There is a situation which demands investigation and clearing up, before we shall convince the Canadian people that we are engaged in an all-out war effort. It is because I know that it is in this field of our war effort, particularly, that this discontent exists, that I urge the. government to give to the electors some knowledge of what steps it proposes to take for the mobilization of wealth and industry, before it asks the voters for a blank cheque for the mobilization of manpower.
Let me repeat that the government need have no fear of the plebiscite vote, provided it is prepared to adopt a bolder and much more far-reaching policy in regard to wealth and industry. The people of Canada to-day are clamouring loudly for bold government leadership, leadership whioh will give us the only policy worthy of our cause, a policy which will mobilize everything we have for the winning of the war.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not intended saying anything in the debate at this point, but there were some observations by the Secretary of State (Mr. McLarty) which I felt called for some comment, before I see passage of the resolution.
Before dealing with the subject in hand, however, I should like to extend to the hon. member who last spoke my sincere congratulations upon the ability he has shown as a parliamentarian. Certainly one can see that his election means a distinct acquisition to the debating power of the house as a whole, and I am sure the party to which he belongs have every reason to feel great satisfaction at his accession to their group.
I hope I have misunderstood some of the words used by the Secretary of State in explaining the provisions of the measure. It seems to me that in Canada we have not gone as far
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Tucker

as we should have by this time in building up a distinct sense of Canadian nationality and citizenship. There has been far too much emphasis laid upon racial origin of people who have come to our country in past generations, and who have shown thedr desire to be good citizens. Indeed I think far too much emphasis has been laid upon the suggestion that we have two great races in Canada because, from what I can see, the French race in Canada is, after all, very closely related to the English race in Canada. I doubt very much whether we have in fact two distinct races in Canada, and it is my belief that we of those two races are closely united in racial origin. If we were to get away from that idea of thinking so much of racial origin, It would be better for Canada as a whole.
I hope, as I have said, that I misunderstood the Secretary of State when I thought I heard him say that any person resident in Canada whose racial origin was that of a country at war with Canada, and who was disfranchised by a law of any legislature in Canada, would not be permitted to vote on the plebiscite anywhere. I hope I am mistaken in my understanding, because I can see tremendous repercussions from such a provision in the law. We may know now what provisions there may be in the provincial laws; but, as I understand it, once we legislate that way, if at any time before the voting takes place any provincial legislature chooses to disfranchise the people whose racial origin is that of any country with which we are at war-no matter how long those people may have lived in Canada, or how many generations they may have lived here-they would be disfranchised by this particular section.
We should go very slowly when writing any such provision into the statutes of our country. I am prepared to trust the government of Canada, but I am not prepared to trust what any single legislature in Canada might do. driven on by some of the leadership which at times they have displayed. Just to show the danger of that kind of legislation, let me put this to the house: Let us suppose-and God forbid that it should happen-that before the voting takes place Hitler drives Vichy France to war against us. Let us suppose, further, that some legislature in Canada passes an act stipulating that no person of enemy origin shall have any right to vote on the plebiscite. Under such circumstances, in what position would this parliament be placed?
There is no suggestion as to how far back we should go, in tracing racial origin. Are we to go back one generation, two generations, five generations or ten? I protest against the division of Canadians into groups having certain racial origins.

There are in Canada many hundreds of thousands of people of German origin, who are just as loyal to Canada as any member of the house. What would happen if some legislature passed an act whereby a person of German origin were not permitted to vote? Under the explanation given by the Secretary of State those people, whose sons may be serving in the army, whose husbands may be in the army, would be disfranchised by an act of this parliament.
I do not wish it to be understood that I am becoming hysterical about such legislation, but I cannot help thinking about the tremendous amount of harm done in 1917 by similar legislation. People who were loyal citizens of Canada felt tremendously hurt when they were not permitted to exercise the ordinary duties and rights of citizenship at the time of the war-time election. Before the bill is placed before the house by a Liberal government, I urge that any discrimination on racial grounds should be stricken from it.
I know of dozens of people within my own constituency who undoubtedly are of German racial origin, and who are serving in the armed forces of this dominion. Are we to say that their fathers or their brothers are not to have the right to vote, the same as any other person in the country? I know there are many people who will vote either in favour of or against the plebiscite, when the time comes, who will know there will be no chance of their being conscripted. Why make any discrimination on racial grounds? If a man is a good citizen of Canada, if he has done no harm, and if he is expected to discharge the obligations of citizenship, then I submit he should be given all the rights connected therewith. Under the National Resources Mobilization Act there is no discrimination as to racial origin. Young men of German origin are expected to serve their country the same as people of other origins. Thank God that, so far as that measure was concerned, there was no discrimination against people of different racial origins. If they are good Canadians, we treat them as such.
In the present instance are we to say to people of German origin, "Yes, you are' good citizens; we expect you to defend the country; we expect you to obey the call and to offer your lives, if necessary, in its defence; but we will not give you the right to vote on a problem like this." I suggest that our government should not introduce an act which might do such a thing.
Then there is the vexed question respecting conscientious objectors-a most difficult question. But I know, too, that many of our Mennonite groups have suggested to the government that they are quite ready to enter

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
the armed services, provided they are permitted to do non-combatant work. They are willing to go into the ambulance service, the hospital service, labour battalions and so on. as long as they will not have to go against their conscientious beliefs and actually fight or kill their fellowmen. The attitude has been taken that there is no such thing as a non-combatant in this war and that, therefore, unless a man is willing to go and kill his fellowmen, he shall not be permitted to enter the armed forces. He cannot go and be a stretcher-bearer or do hospital work; he must go on the basis of being prepared to do anything he is ordered to do in the way of killing.
In passing I suggest, with all deference to our own military leaders, that this has not been the attitude of the great President of the United States. I saw myself an order which he signed, that conscientious objectors who are willing to serve their country, could do so in non-combatant branches of the armed services of the United States. I saw a copy of an order signed by the chief of staff of the United States stating what branches these conscientious objectors would be able to serve in. But we are saying that conscientious objectors who are willing to go into the armed services of the crown and risk their lives in those armed services, just because they are not wilLing to go in on terms whereby they may be required to fight and kill, shall not have the right to vote on this question. I know dozens of good young friends of mine, who belong to the Mennonite faith, who have gone into Red Cross work in the army, trusting that they will not be asked to bear arms. Many have gone into the Royal Canadian Air Force. By this very measure-and I ask every member of the house to consider what we are doing-the relatives of these young men will be prevented from voting unless they say they are ready to go into the armed forces and be prepared to go and kill, against their religious beliefs.
The reason why I have spoken at this particular stage is that I want the government to reconsider the question of introducing a bill with any provisions like that in it. I call back to memory the shades of great leaders of Liberalism who fought against similar provisions in the War-time Elections Act of 1917. I cannot begin to echo, with anything like their eloquence, the sentiments which they voiced in support of the principle that when you give a man citizenship you should not deprive him of the rights of citizenship. I hold ini my hand the Hansard in which those great speeches were made, and I ask this government in all sincerity, and
in the hope that it will not embarrass them in any way, that before they introduce in the house a bill embodying any such provision, they reconsider the matter and refrain from taking a step which I think, on more mature consideration, and especially in the light of the teachings of Liberalism, they would consider inconsistent with those great teachings.

I wish to say a few words on the resolution before it passes, but before I refer to the resolution itself, may I extend my congratulations to the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworbhy) who took his seat in the house for the first time on Wednesday last.
I think he made a good job of his speech, and I do not believe he will need assistance from others so far as his work in this house is concerned. He seems quite able to take care of himself.
As regards the general principle of going to the country on a plebiscite, we have no objection when it involves a matter of policy or principle; but I certainly have an objection to this particular plebiscite because it is most evasive, and I cannot see any good result that will come from it. I have heard over and over again in this house the statement that the government was asking to be released from its commitment. That is not right. The government is not asking to be released from a commitment. Let us see what it asks? The plebiscite is worded thus:
Are you in favour of releasing the government from any obligation arising out of any past commitments restricting the methods of raising men for military service?
That is an entirely different matter. It is asking people if they are in favour of releasing the government; but the government is not asking to be released. There is quite a distinction there, a great difference. It simply puts the government in this position, that if the people express their desire of releasing the government from its commitments, the government can sit right down and do nothing. It is not asking to be released, and in that regard the government is perfectly within its rights to go on and do exactly as it has done in the past. I spoke on this particular question before, and it is my considered opinion that the government does not intend to change its policy. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) told us that in his speech when he first spoke in this house. I referred to the remarks of the late Minister of Justice, Mr. Lapointe; I also referred to the remarks of the present Minister of Public Works (Mr. Cardin) and to the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power). When the late Mr. Lapointe, then Minister of Justice, was
"94	COMMONS
Plebiscite Act-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
speaking in this house, he told the people of Quebec and the members of the house, in no uncertain terms, that there would never, never, never be conscription; and the Minister of Public Works was one of those to whom he referred. The hon. gentleman is sitting in his place now and I ask him to correct me if I am wrong. Mr. Lapointe said: "I speak for Mr. Cardin and I speak for Mr. Power; we will leave the government before there will be any conscription put into effect in this dominion."
I should like to hear the Minister of Public Works contradict that statement if I am wrong. I sincerely believe I am right in this. In my opinion it is a wrong attitude for the government to take, and that is why I will oppose this particular plebiscite. If they can convince me that they really intend to do something on this thing, then it is an entirely different matter.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: Does the hon. member object to putting the government in a position where it could do something if it considered it necessary?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: The government, under the mobilization act, can do anything it likes. If the question were put in a positive way on this plebiscite, then there would be some sense in it. But the government is definitely not doing that. It will be recalled that when I was speaking before, I pointed out that there were two sides to the question of the plebiscite-one was meant for the French-speaking people of Quebec and the other for the English-speaking people of the other provinces. I do not think anything could be done that would create greater disunity in the country than that very thing. If the French people of Quebec and the Englishspeaking people of the rest of Canada were given clearly to understand our situation, clearly to understand that this government intended to go all-out, that it intended to mobilize completely finance and material resources, right to the last man and the last dollar, I believe that the people of Quebec- because I have spoken in that province many times, and I know them-would agree for an all-out war effort.

speechtext: You have not made much impression.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
Well, you have not made such a hot impression either. I am sure that the people of Quebec would be just as enthusiastically behind an all-out war effort as those of any other province. I do not blame the people of Quebec for being a little cautious as to the promises which this
TMr. C. E. Johnston.]
government has given, because the rest of us elsewhere in Canada have sound reasons for being a little suspicious of its promises.
This whole question is not one which has come up overnight. When I hear some hon. members speaking in this chamber I am almost led to believe that in their opinion this issue has risen rather rapidly. Let us make no mistake; this is a political trick; it was begun in 1940; and I am amazed at the shortness of the memory of some hon. members, who cannot even think back to 1939. I well recall the occasion in this house when the party with which I am associated asked for an all-out war effort. Some of us were told that we were committing political suicide, and in fact we lost seven of our members.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext: But we were right.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR TAKING OF VOTES ON ANY QUESTION SUBMITTED BY WAY PLEBISCITE
speechtext:
We were
right, yes, and every member in this house realizes it now. We had to take a lot of abuse because of our stand on behalf of the unity of Canada. Then this question came up in 1940, when the issue of conscription of man-power was fought on every political platform. We of this group advocated first of all a complete mobilization-conscription, if you like-of the financial institutions, so that we would be able, if I may use the Prime Minister's own words, to issue currency and credit in terms of public need. But when we put that resolution before the house everyone outside our party voted against it. Those who did so may have been sincere, and I am not going to say they were not, but I do affirm that it showed a decided lack of leadership in that critical time, in 1940, when the issue was being discussed.
The government is now trying to have the people say whether they wish to release it, but the government is not asking for release. To my mind it is another political trick, and shows very poor leadership; nothing indeed is more calculated to disunite the country. If the government has misjudged the necessities of the case, and can do nothing better than ask the people if they would like to release it, I say we have no time for such fooling around as that. If the Prime Minister, with all. due respect to his ability as a leader, has not sufficient vision, foresight and leadership to conduct Canada through this most critical time in its history, then I humbly say to you, Mr. Speaker, that he should resign and make way for someone else who can. We know that a man is not necessarily to be blamed for mistakes he may make, but certainly you cannot expect a country to put its trust in a person who continually makes mistakes, and this government is notorious for the mistakes it has

Plebiscite Act-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
made since this war broke out. I do not believe there is another government in the whole world which has made such colossal mistakes as this particular government has.

Yes. The people will get that, too. But the thing with
which we are primarily concerned., and have been ever since this war started., is an all-out war effort. We have not been concerned so much with political tricks as my hon. friends across the floor who are interrupting just now. That is the sort of thing which creates disunity. It leads to the sort of disorganization of which we have evidence in the laying off of five hundred men from an Ottawa plant. Were we wrong when we asked for complete mobilization of the natural and industrial resources of this country? All over Canada industrial capacity and industrial workers are standing idle, although those concerned are only too anxious to get to work. Just the day before yesterday I got a letter from an important executive of one of the aircraft factories. The situation he pointed out to me is appalling. He stated that in his factory a large number of men were laid off. Nearly all of them were expert mechanics, who have been working on the production of war supplies for the last year or two. It was pointed out to me that these men are now either enlisting in the army or seeking other jobs, and that when this company is asked to return to full production it will not be able to do so, because it will not have the experienced men. Yet we are supposed to be engaged in an all-out war effort. One of our greatest deficiencies is in the matter of production. I heard the Prime Minister say the other day that we shall probably not be permitted to discuss this subject in the secret session. Yet to me it is a matter of more concern than any other. I am not going to question .the judgment of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) as to whether Bren guns should be sent to Singapore, or to Australia, or should be kept here. He is a military man, and in that I will accept his judgment. But the thing I am concerned about is this: Let us get the guns made. To say that we are manufacturing 4,500 Bren guns a month is not the point at all, because if we are manufacturing 4.500 Bren guns a month and we can bring that production up to 9,000 or 90,000 Bren guns a month, or whatever the figure may be-if we can double the present output, that is what we should be doing. If we are building a certain number of corvettes within a given time, and we could with proper organization build twice that number within the same time, that is what we should be doing.

Yes, as my hon. friend the member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) says, if we could put out even one more a month, that is what we should be doing. Then we would at least be endeavouring to have an all-out war effort. Can you

envisage, Mr. Speaker, the government telling us that they do not even now know how many factories are working full-time? I think it is unpardonable that a government should be in such a position after almost three years of war organization, that they do not know yet how many factories are working full-time and how many are working only part-time. That is the greatest criticism I have to offer of the government at the moment.
In submitting the plebiscite, I cannot see why the government does not make it a positive question rather than a negative one. Certainly they should seek direction, and direct direction, from the people, so that the people will know without question what is going to happen. Why in the world cannot the government be honest about this matter and say to the people: We want you to release us from this pledge so that we can have conscription for overseas if necessary? But that has never been said yet. I have not found it in the Prime Minister's address. The question submitted seems to evade that. Or, if we are not going to have conscription, let us be honest and say so. I do not think there is any danger of frightening the people to such an extent that they are going to become panicky and run away from the enemy if we tell them the truth. I do not mean that they should be told military secrets such as the transport of troops and matters of that kind. But tell them the exact situation in other matters and you will find out that the people are right behind you. They are behind you now, pushing so hard that you do not know where to go. That is the trouble-they are pushing you too much.

Mr. Speaker, this is an appropriate moment at which to raise a point of order which has been in my mind in the course of this debate. I direct the attention of the house to the fact that the present motion is one necessitated by the fact that a bill is about to be introduced which will place a charge upon the public revenue. Being a bill of that nature it is recommended to the house in the first instance by His Excellency the Governor General. Being recommended by his excellency in the form in which it appears, the motion cannot be amended. That is the first point I wish to make, namely, that the amendment is entirely out of order for the reason given.
Not being capable of amendment, it is, I think, sound constitutional procedure that the motion should not be debatable. Debate on a motion of this nature, unless there is some other governing factor, is, or ought to be, out of order at the present time.
I would direct the attention of hon. members to standing order 60 on page 161 of Beauchesne:
Motion imposing public aid or charge.
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned till such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
Standing order 60 certainly would rule out the debate that has thus far taken place upon this resolution, and it illustrates in the best manner possible why a rule of this kind should be construed literally. Most of the discussion that has taken place thus far I think I am right in saying has been a repetition of what took place in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do not think there has been a single point raised in the speeches thus far made on this matter which was not raised in one form or another in the debate on the address.

But he and I alike I think are interested in seeing that the rules of the house are strictly construed, and particularly those placed there with a view to expediting the business of parliament. There is the strongest of reasons in connection with the very matter we are debating at the moment, namely, the wording of a plebiscite, why the matter should be decided by this house as quickly as possible. We have been told over and over again in the course of the debate that every moment's delay in getting the plebiscite before the people may occasion great concern at the end and is to be very much regretted. There will be an opportunity to debate all phases of the plebiscite question on the bill when it is before the house, and there will be opportunity when the resolution has been passed to ask questions on the resolution when the house is in committee of the whole. I do submit that the time to expect answers to questions on a resolution of this kind is not in the course of debate on the resolution itself, but only when the resolution is before the committee of the whole house.
I raise the point at this stage because, while I am free to say that I think the house in past years has frequently ignored this standing order, there has come to be almost a custom, when a motion of the kind preceding a money bill is introduced, of having a debate on the resolution itself. I think the intention of the rule was to avoid anything of the kind; that the whole purpose of a resolution is to secure time for hon. members to see the importance of the matter to be dealt with involving expenditure of public moneys, and to be afforded opportunity in committee to raise questions and receive answers before the bill is introduced. But the debate on the subject of the bill should take place on the bill itself rather than on a resolution preceding its introduction.

With respect to the first point I am in agreement, inasmuch as the bill is a money bill. On that I shall not elaborate. But on the second point I take distinct issue with the Prime Minister. He is reading into standing order 60 something that is not there. Unless he reads something into it that is not there, there is no point or force in his argument. I am astonished that the question has been raised here to-day, because I cannot recall a point of order like this having been taken on a money resolution pre-
Plebiscite Act-Point of Order

ceding a bill in the last twenty years. I should be astonished if the Prime Minister can find a single precedent. Certainly there is nothing in the standing order which says there shall be no debate. What it says is that:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon . . .
That is, you cannot enter upon it without notice from the governor general, as I understand. the implications of that. But that having been given, then the motion is moved and debate ensues thereon. The question of referring it to the committee follows after that debate has taken place and the motion carried.
It is a debatable motion; it cannot be anything else. Surely for the last twenty years, and I should think a long time before that, this house has not been going wrong on a matter of this kind.
I think the first point taken is a proper point of order and this amendment must fail on that ground, but certainly not on the second ground. I would be astonished if that were the proper interpretation of the rule. You cannot construe a statute strictly by reading something into it, and a rule of the House of Commons is by analogy in the nature of a statute. On the other hand I think it ought to be construed liberally, and certainly this debate is in order and should go on.
I understand, of course, that that is not the primary reason for the Prime Minister rising at this time; he has risen because of the intervention of this proposed amendment. I think he is right on his first ground, but on the second ground I most respectfully dissent from him.

It is clear, therefore, that the resolution must be transmitted to the committee of the whole in the terms recommended to the house by the message of the governor general, and the amendment proposed is therefore out of order; and I so rule.
The next question is that raised by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) who quoted standing order 60 and submitted that the resolution before the house is not debatable. With this standing order, however, must be read standing order 38, which provides, inter alia:
(1) The following motions are debatable:
Every motion
(a) standing on the order of proceedings for the day.
The resolution is on the order of proceedings for the day. I would point out that standing order 60 was passed in 1867, while standing order 38 was passed on March 22, 1927. In other words, standing order 38 is remedial to standing order 60, and I must conclude that standing order 38 must rule, and decide that the resolution before the house is debatable.
What extent may be allowed in the debate is a much more difficult problem. All that is asked of the house is that the Speaker leave the chair for the house to resolve itself into committee of the whole.
The debate, therefore, must be directed to the negative of that motion, that the resolution should not be submitted to the committee of the whole, for, as I have pointed out, no amendment at this stage can be in order.
