speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister of Public Works
subtopic: AUTHORIZATION OF PAYMENT OF $100,000 FOR THE YEAR ENDING JULY 1, 1942
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this is the resolution preceding the introduction of a bill for payment to the city of Ottawa of the sum of $100,000 as the result of an agreement which was reached between the city of Ottawa and the federal government a number of years ago in settlement of claims which had been put forward by the city for compensation for loss of revenue on properties which the federal government had acquired, and which left the city of Ottawa short of a certain amount of tax revenue. The claim of the city of Ottawa, as I stated last year and the house will remember, was for a very much larger amount than this, but as a result of discussions between the Department of Public Works and representatives of the city of Ottawa an agreement was reached that all parties concerned would be satisfied with a payment by the federal government to the city of Ottawa of $100,000 a year. This agreement has been renewed, if my memory serves me aright, for ten or fifteen years. I might add that representations have been made by the city of Ottawa that we should increase the amount, but in view of the war it was thought advisable to leave the situation as it is and not to undertake negotiations for a new agreement in place of the original agreement authorized in 1920 at $75,000 and which ran from July 1, 1919, to July 1, 1924, was renewed for one year to 1925, renewed for a period of five years from 1925 to 1930 at $100,000, and has been renewed year by year since 1930 at $100,000.

Has the minister not taken into consideration the vast expansion in the services rendered by the city of Ottawa and the large number of buildings and properties taken over by the federal government, which make a very great change indeed in the services rendered by the city to the government? I think this agreement was first entered into approximately twenty years ago, when the services rendered by the city of Ottawa to the dominion government, and the -city property acquired by the government were very much less than now. The situation has changed vastly since the agreement was first entered into, and in fact within the last year or two the water supply situation, in view of the services rendered by the city of Ottawa, is critical, calling for an expansion of the water service. It is a matter that should be given much more than perfunctory consideration in order that an equitable agreement may be arrived at between the dominion government and the city of Ottawa in view of the revenue-producing properties to the city which

City of Ottawa Agreement

have been taken over by the government and the very much greater services rendered by the corporation. In view of these factors I think it would only be fair to the city of Ottawa that serious consideration be given - by the federal government to making an equitable adjustment at this time. The excuse that we are at war and that economy is demanded surely does not apply to a situation such as prevails in this capital city of Canada. I would ask the Minister of Public Works to give the committee a few more particulars, showing the changes between the services rendered twenty or twenty-five years ago when this agreement was first entered into, and the services rendered to-day.

The minister has spoken about the amount of water used in the public buildings. I think that what my colleague had to say was about the increased water supply which is necessary for fire protection in the city, due to the erection on Wellington street of a number of very inflammable wooden buildings, which constitute, in my judgment, a serious fire hazard and a menace to the safety of the city. I am not criticizing the government for having built wooden buildings there; everything had to be done hastily. The Department of Munitions and Supply grew up overnight, as it were, and had to have accommodation, and no doubt wooden accommodation was the easiest and most quickly available method. Nevertheless, it constitutes a grave fire hazard to the city of Ottawa.
But that is not the main factor to which, I think, he should direct his attention; it is the direct loss sustained by the city treasury by reason of such buildings as, let us say, the Jackson building, which has been expropriated by the government, and which, as I understand the law, automatically comes off the assessment roll; and by the expropriation of the Brading brewery building at the lower end of Wellington street. I do not suggest that the city of Ottawa has lost a great deal on the assessment roll by reason of the Brading property being taken over, because the assessment on the building, land, and appurtenances was very moderate compared with the sum this government paid. I know the answer will be that that was an exchequer court judgment. I wonder whether hon. members know just how the amount was arrived at. I believe the sum paid was. $550,000 on the basis of the exchequer court award. But it was a sham battle; the government offered in the expropriation proceedings to pay the $550,000 odd; the company in filing its defence accepted the offer, and there never was a jot or tittle of evidence taken to support the claim, one way or the other. It was a cloak behind which the government may shelter itself if it desires to justify the payment of so huge a sum for-what shall I term it?-that hole in the ground down there on Wellington street. I am going to have something more to say about that later on. It ought to have been said long ago.

subtopic: REPEAL OF PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT

speechtext: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (for the Minister of National Revenue) moved the second reading of Bill No. 2, to repeal the Petroleum and Naphtha Inspection Act.

subtopic: REPEAL OF PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT
speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: REPEAL OF PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT
speechtext:
This bill stands, it will be
observed, in the name of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson), but unfortunately my colleague is indisposed this evening, and in order to facilitate the business of the house I am undertaking this task. I must confess, however, that I really do not know a great deal about the bill. The explanatory note reveals the purpose of the measure. It is a repeal measure entirely. Apparently the original act was passed in 1877, which provided for certain forms of inspection. I am not able to give the house the details, but I presume, inspection of wells producing petroleum and naphtha, and also of factories or industrial establishments processing the same. Apparently the inspection has passed out of usage. I judge from the explanatory note that the regulations of municipal and provincial bodies regarding this inspection have superseded the inspection requirements contemplated under the act of 1877, and therefore there is no need of retaining that measure on the statute books. So this bill is introduced to repeal it.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. B. HANSON (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: REPEAL OF PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT
speechtext:
I have some observations to make on this bill. I recall that in introducing the bill the minister gave a brief explanation in which he laid it down as a principle that the provisions of the act were obsolete and outmoded. That, I think, is largely true, but there are one or two things in that act which ought to be retained, and when I call attention to them, and the department and the
minister give consideration to them, I believe their retention will be found desirable.
A word on the drafting of the bill. It is a repealing section. It is declaratory, and I suggest the insertion of the word "hereby"- "is hereby repealed". I do not know that that is important, but it is better drafting.
The explanatory note reads:
Practically all the operative provisions of this act have been superseded by other acts and regulations of municipal, provincial or federal origin. . . .
Anyone who reviews the whole act, as I took occasion to do the other day, will agree that many sections were designed to meet conditions existing when the act was passed, away back before I was born, and owing to changes in these conditions the majority of the sections have not much if any importance to-day. But it occurs to me in reading the act that there are three or four sections which are still of importance, and which, so far as I am aware, are not duplicated by any other act of the federal parliament. I believe the minister should examine some of these sections and explain why it is not proposed to retain them.
Take, for example, section 3:
3.	The governor in council may, from time to time, make such regulations respecting the storage and possession of petroleum and naphtha as lie deems necessary for the public safety, and may make special regulations as to the importation or possession of naphtha and as to the sale thereof and use for illuminating purposes;
Then sections 4 and 5 seem to me worthy of retention:
4. The governor in council may, from time to time, designate places at which petroleum may be imported in tank cars and in tank ships respectively. . . .
5.	The department may make regulations, not inconsistent with the provisions of this act, with respect to the transportation, shipment or sale of imported or domestic petroleum or naphtha.
I assume that both sections have been operative in the past. Powers similar to those contained in these sections are now, I believe, vested in the oil controller under an order in council passed pursuant to the War Measures Act. But I point out to the house and to the Minister of National Revenue that these powers of the oil controller are of a transitory nature, and that at the close of the war and upon the disappearance of the War Measures Act these powers will disappear. Should there not rest in some governmental body some power to regulate the storage and possession of petroleum, which power would continue in peace time? If you repeal this statute there is no power. This deo.'e with

I do not know under just what authority that is done; I know that in my own community we try to keep them as far away from the residential district as possible in order to keep down the fire hazard. But if sections 3, 4 and 5 are repealed, there will then be no one authority charged with the responsibility of making regulations about the conditions of storage of this most inflammable material. I do not think such an authority is necessary. I am just assuming that; I have not looked up the constitutional aspect. But I do suggest-and I offer this suggestion in the utmost good faith -that this power of control over storage and all the other things to which these sections refer should be retained in the post-war period. I think I have only to mention that to bring home to the minister the advisability of its being done. Somebody ought to have that authority. Perhaps there is some other authority; I do not know. At the moment the only authority I know of is the oil controller; and I do suggest to the minister- and this is a concrete suggestion to which I hope he will direct his colleague's attention- that these sections should be retained and perhaps redrafted to meet modern conditions.
I can give the minister an additional reason, from a local point of view. Some time ago there was drawn to my attention what was stated to be a serious situation in connection with the storage of petroleum products in Vancouver. I was told that this situation constituted a serious hazard to the people of that city, particularly in the event of air raids. I do not know what may have been done to rectify the situation, but what I have in mind is that there should be an act of this parliament which would empower the federal government to take direct steps in an instance of the kind to which I have referred, which might threaten the safety of a large number of people. I spoke of that before.
Then a question of some importance arises from the fact that this act was actually suspended by order in council P.C. 4-5204, passed on July 16, 1941, under the provisions of the War Measures Act. I assume it was found necessary to do so because of the, shall I

It would appear by every criterion that it was an abuse of the War Measures Act to use it in order to suspend the operations of a peace-time act of parliament. The conditions which led the governor in council to approve passage of the order in council of July 16 last surely must have been evident when parliament was in session last year, since adjournment did not take place until June 14.
I think the position ought to be reviewed, and I believe the minister will see that there is merit in the statute if these three sections are re-drafted and brought up to date. subtopic: REPEAL OF PETROLEUM AND NAPHTHA INSPECTION ACT
speechtext: I should like to say a word on this bill. When the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Gibson) spoke on the matter previously he said that the bill was being brought down in order to stop the adulteration of petroleum and naphtha. To-day it is not a question of adulteration; the refineries are stepping up the gasoline so high that it is really dangerous, and we need an act to protect us. The Germans and Japanese are using gasoline with an octane rating of about 87. Canada and the United States are using gasoline with an octane rating of about 100. In order to step it up not only do they refine the gasoline to a higher degree; they put in propanes and other substances which bring it up to an anti-knock rating, and higher. These propanes have a freezing point of about 45 degrees below zero. That is all right when they are used in an aeroplane or an automobile, because the gases from the propane will sink to the bottom; but if this gasoline is used in a fishing boat, or any other boat, those gases will stay in the hull and cause explosions. This law should protect the fishermen from the danger of explosions caused by the use of propane in our gasoline. Therefore I believe this act ought to be revised all the way through, to take care of the sort of gasoline we are using to-day.

But 1 think it will be found that matters concerning the inspection of oil wells, and everything having to do with them, come under provincial jurisdiction. I happen to know, for instance, that in Alberta, where in recent years there has been a substantial oil development, the provincial government does pass regulations regarding storage, transportation within the province, and like matters. I fancy these come within their jurisdiction, probably wholly so. I have just one other comment to make, and that is with regard to the observations by the leader of the opposition in invoking the War Measures Act to pass certain regulations to set aside provisions of an act which was very largely, if not entirely, obsolete. I do not think, on reflection, that any hon. member would dispute that it is necessary to have direct control,.through the oil controller, over the movement of oil and gasoline when we are at war. It is quite true, as my hon. friend has said, that the provisions of that measure will lapse with the declaration of peace. But I do not believe his criticism was altogether deserved when he found fault with the government for taking steps under the War Measures Act to bring about a proper regulation of this matter in war time, and not proceeding by way of an amending act in the house.
Sometimes I am concerned with the extent of the powers which have to be used arbitrarily by the executive in war time. But we are in a war, and decisions frequently have to be made with a great deal of celerity. Time will not wait. I can assure my hon. friend and the committee that the government always has in mind the exercising of these powers in the public interest; and our good faith in that respect will have to be the justification for our actions.

subtopic: REINSTATEMENT IN CIVIL EMPLOYMENT OF PERSONS WHO ENLIST IN HIS MAJESTY'S FORCES

speechtext:
Hon. HUMPHREY MITCHELL (Minister of Labour) moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, to provide for the reinstatement in civil employment of individuals who enlist for sendee in his majesty's forces or who perform essential war employment.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this bill replaces an order in council similar in content to the bill now before the house. The bill, in turn, is similar to legislation now existing in Great Britain, New Zealand, Australia and the United States, although it follows more closely the legislation in Great Britain.
This bill provides for the orderly reinstatement, at the conclusion of hostilities, of men who have served in the forces on sea, on land or in the air. It also provides penalties for breaches of the provisions. It also provides that where agreements exist between employers and employees, on a mutual basis, provided those agreements are not less advantageous than the act itself, they shall be permitted to remain in effect.
